cards.text: Proverbs keeps rolling, and a father is still teaching his son, same as last chapter (Prov 4:1). He opens with "My son, pay attention to my wisdom." Translation: phone DOWN, friend, Dad's got something important.

cards.question: Why does the father want his son listening so closely?

answers.text: To earn a seat with the elders
To grow rich before he is old

cards.text: Then he warns about the forbidden woman. Though her lips drip honey and her speech is smoother than oil, friend, that's a text that says CONGRATULATIONS YOU WON, and you never entered ANYTHING.

cards.question: Honey and oil at the start. But the father says that in the end the forbidden woman is ___.
Bitter as wormwood and sharp as a double-edged sword. So where do the forbidden woman's steps lead?
The forbidden woman carefully considers the path of life.

cards.text: She doesn't even know her ways are unstable. Reminds me of my first week on this gold base, hopping around like a PRO when I was really just a wobble with a mustache.
So now the father turns to "my sons" and tells them to listen and not turn aside from what he's saying.

cards.question: The father's game plan for dealing with the forbidden woman: keep your path ___ from her.

cards.text: Don't even go near the door of her house. That's me and the snooze button: if the phone's on the nightstand, I LOSE, so the phone sleeps across the room.

cards.question: The father warns that going near the forbidden woman could hand the son's years to someone cruel.
If the son goes near her door, who ends up feasting on his wealth?

cards.text: Then the father skips ahead to the end of the son's life. His flesh and his body are spent, and he groans.

cards.question: Groaning at the end of his life, what does the son finally admit?

answers.text: He hated discipline and ignored his teachers
He never had anyone to teach him
He worked too hard and rested too little

cards.text: "I did not listen to the voice of my teachers." Friend, that's me skipping the instructions, building the whole shelf, then staring at THREE extra screws.

cards.question: The groaning son says he's on the brink of ruin all alone where nobody can see.

cards.text: Then the father switches pictures to water. He says, "Drink water from your own cistern, and running water from your own well."

cards.question: In the father's water picture, what is he telling the son to do?

answers.text: Stay with what is his own
Find his water in the city

cards.text: He asks, "Why should your springs flow in the streets, your streams of water in the public squares?" That's leaving your front door wide open with a sign that says HELP YOURSELF.

cards.question: The father says the son's streams of water should be shared with strangers.

cards.text: Then the father says may your fountain be blessed. And now the water picture gets personal.

cards.question: The father says the son should find his joy in his ___.

cards.text: He calls her a loving doe, a graceful fawn, and says may you be captivated by her love forever. Friend, this isn't a lecture anymore, it's a WEDDING TOAST.

cards.question: After that toast about the wife of his youth, what does the father ask his son?

answers.text: Why be captivated by an adulteress
Why trust the advice of strangers
Why waste your years on hard work

cards.question: The father says the LORD sees only some of a man's paths.

cards.text: A man's ways are before the eyes of the LORD, and He examines all his paths. No incognito tab, friend. ALL of them.

cards.question: The father finishes by talking about the wicked man. What traps him?

cards.text: The cords of his sin entangle him. That's me with a phone charger I tangled up MYSELF, yelling at a knot I tied.

cards.question: In the end, the wicked man dies for lack of ___.

cards.text: He's led astray by his own great folly. And there's that word again, discipline, the same one the groaning son said he hated.

findings.problem: The question sets up the blank with "Honey and oil at the start. But the father says..." The word "But" signals a contrast with honey and oil, which rules out the wrong answer "sweeter" before the baker has to reason about it.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The question links verse 4 to verse 5 with "So," as if her steps lead to death because she is bitter and sharp. The text doesn't make that cause-and-effect link.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The right answer "Down to death" is a state. The wrong answers "Down to Egypt" and "Up to Bethel" are map places. The right answer stands out as the only one of its kind.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: The wrong answer "close" makes the line read "keep your path close from her." That is ungrammatical, and no one would believe it in the middle of a warning to stay away. It is a throwaway option.

rule.text: Wrong answers for what someone does or says only need to be believable.

findings.problem: This story card re-quotes Proverbs 5:13 ("I did not listen to the voice of my teachers"). Card 14 already covered that verse in its right answer, so this card adds a joke but doesn't move the passage forward.
Verse 18 is a wish: "may you rejoice in the wife of your youth." The question turns it into an instruction: "the son should find his joy in his ___."

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: This story card retells Proverbs 5:21 ("A man's ways are before the eyes of the LORD, and He examines all his paths"). Card 9 just covered that verse, so the card recaps instead of moving the passage forward.
"No incognito tab, friend." This sits in a passage about adultery and sexual temptation. Hiding a private browser tab there reads as a suggestive hint about what someone might be hiding.

rule.text: No cursing, crude humor, innuendo, or social or political commentary.

findings.problem: Several self-deprecating jokes put Papa Dorin in modern human situations outside his bakery. In Stop 1 card 10, he keeps his phone on a nightstand and fights the snooze button. In Stop 1 card 15, he builds a shelf and ends up with extra screws. In Stop 2 card 12, he tangles a phone charger. papa-dorin.md lets him use everyday adult life for comparisons and lets his jokes make up small moments "around his bakery." It also says he never adds anything new to his world. It doesn't say whether he can claim personal habits like owning a phone or furniture.
findings.question: Can Papa Dorin tell first-person jokes where he owns or uses everyday modern things like a phone, a nightstand or flat-pack furniture? Or should everyday-life comparisons be about people in general ("That's like someone who..."), with his own self-deprecating jokes kept to the bakery, the drawer and the Dorinverse?
